source.title: The Big Sobol Sequence : How many simulations do we need for simulation-based inference in cosmology?
source.authors: A. Bairagi; Benjamin Dan Wandelt; F. Villaescusa-Navarro

record.tranche_reason: The study tests power-law-like scaling in cosmological neural-network training, a setting different from language-model pretraining. It varies the number of training simulations and reports held-out loss and posterior-estimation results.
record.gate_note: The study does not test language-model loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute, or compute-optimal allocation. Its scaling-law citations are background, not results from those cited studies. Its own results concern cosmological inference as the training-set size changes.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws with an irreducible term to held-out loss versus training-set size for MLP regressors and neural posterior estimators on cosmological simulations. That is a non-text setting, so it bears on V5. It does not vary model parameters or compute for language models, so V1–V4 and V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add that the authors conclude existing suites (Quijote LH, 2,000 simulations) are too small for networks to reach the Cramér-Rao bound even for P(k). The LH-based power-law prediction of about 4,000 simulations was confirmed with the new BSQ suite. Sampling design changes the scaling constants, not the power-law form. Wavelet NPE also shows power-law KL-loss scaling. More simulations often help more than more layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies cosmological simulation training-set size and measures regression loss, Fisher information, and posterior-estimation results; it does not use the language-model pretraining scaling-law setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The Latin Hypercube and Sobol sampling designs produce different loss constants and slightly different test losses; the paper attributes this potentially to parameter-space sampling. Network depth and training-set size also affect information extraction and optimization difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Sobol vs Latin Hypercube sampling changes the constant of the data-scaling law (BSQ test loss is higher at equal N), while exponents agree within 10% (0.36 vs 0.39).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-size scaling for simulation-based inference, training-set sampling design shifts the scaling constant but leaves the exponent roughly unchanged.

fits_no_version.finding: Neural-summary Fisher information approaches the P(k) optimum as training simulations grow, saturating near 4,000 BSQ simulations. LH at 500–1,500 simulations does not saturate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In cosmological neural inference, extracted information saturates the summary's Cramér-Rao bound at a training-set size predictable from loss scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Posterior constraints on Ωm and σ8 tighten markedly with more simulations; other parameters tighten mildly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In wavelet-based neural posterior estimation, posterior constraints improve with training-set size, unevenly across parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Similar Fisher information can be reached by more simulations or more depth. Depth gains plateau at 6 hidden layers, and deeper nets are harder to optimise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In cosmological MLP inference, depth and training-set size trade off, with depth gains plateauing.

record.problems: The study is a cosmological-inference case study rather than a language-model study. Numerical fit uncertainties are not stated, and the wavelet scaling exponent is not reported in the text. The authors note that test loss is averaged across the prior volume while Fisher information is evaluated at the fiducial point, and that sampling design affects test-loss constants.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters or compute (only training-set size varies). Image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Very large models.
No test of fitting method, parameter counting, schedule, or compute-optimal split. The sampling-design comparison changes data, and the exponents agree within 10% with no uncertainties reported.
Language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude for language models. The study's own extrapolation (1,500 to about 4,000 simulations) is in a different setting and only about 3x.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.

missing.what: An extrapolation test of the LH-fitted law. It predicted several thousand simulations would be needed; BSQ shows information saturating near 4,000. However, BSQ loss sat above the LH curve, and from the offset the authors 'may have expected' about 10,000. This is only about a 3x extrapolation, in a non-LM setting.
missing.locator: Section 5, Fig. 2 caption; Section 5.1, paragraphs on Fig. 5
missing.versions: V2 (only loosely; non-LM setting, small extrapolation) / none

missing.what: The authors report a steeper scaling law for neural posterior estimation than for posterior-mean regression, so the exponent depends on task and loss. No number is given.

record.verdict_notes: This is a cosmology study in which only training-set size varies, with small MLPs and normalizing flows. It bears only on V5, as a non-text data-scaling instance. The reader's V7 link is removed: the exponent difference (0.39 vs 0.36) has no uncertainties, and the authors frame it as agreement. Neither study is an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Language-model loss comparisons at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling with training-simulation count in cosmological parameter inference, including power-spectrum regression and wavelet-based posterior estimation. It does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.

The study compares two simulation-sampling designs and different inference tasks, but does not test language-model fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or compute-optimal allocation. It does not report curves bending away from a power law.

rows.measure: Held-out test loss as a function of training-simulation count

Add that the combined test loss stays above the Cramér-Rao bound and is slightly higher than LH at equal N. rows.subject: Ensemble of neural posterior estimators (MAF, GF, NICE, NSF, and MDN)

rows.value: The log-probability follows a power law; exponent not stated

rows.check: No exponent is given in the text. The conclusion calls this a 'steeper scaling law' than the regression case, with no number. The measure is log-probability of fiducial simulations, reported as KL loss scaling. Training-set sizes are 100–1,500.
